solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique, linked answer split by the grid); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

indicators.note: within says the word for murders sits inside the word for gang

parts.note: a gang or clique is a set
murder's read as 'murder is', i.e. one who murders kills

explanation.surface: A mob killing presented as something a person is capable of doing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'within' is the container signal; the 's of murder's is read as 'is', so the verb form is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: A range of abilities a person has is what that person's capabilities amount to; a near synonym.

clue.text: Didn't meet party leaders — one's upset

indicators.note: one of the two leaders is turned over, so his name is read backwards

parts.note: Dave Cameron led the Conservatives and Ed Miliband led Labour when this was set
the second leader is Ed Miliband of Labour

explanation.surface: Someone skipped a meeting with the heads of a political party, and one of those heads is annoyed.
explanation.walkthrough: The leaders are Cameron and Miliband by first names, as in 2012; 'one's upset' turns only the Tory's name backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To avoid or dodge someone is to fail to meet them, so the past tense matches 'didn't meet'.

indicators.note: catches says one word holds the other inside it

parts.note: doing something unaided is doing it alone
a cap is a player picked for a national team, an international

explanation.surface: A lone hand nabs a crook wanted across borders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'catches' is the container signal; a cap is a player selected for a national side.
explanation.definitionFit: Al Capone was the notorious Chicago gangster of the Prohibition era, a famous example of a criminal.

clue.text: Going to witter on about bribe

indicators.note: about turns the chattering word round so it reads backwards

parts.note: to witter on is to yap, chatter tediously
someone going or leaving is off

explanation.surface: Someone about to ramble on about a bribe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' turns YAP into PAY; 'to' just links the two parts.
explanation.definitionFit: A payment made to buy someone's cooperation dishonestly is a bribe; an idiomatic equivalent.

indicators.note: fighting suggests the letters are in turmoil, thrown about into a new order

explanation.surface: A bold side activity of tackling crime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fighting' rearranges the fourteen letters of DARING SIDELINE.
explanation.definitionFit: Trading shares using confidential information is an offence in law, an example of a crime.

clue.text: Way to identify criminal in suit (not British)

indicators.note: not British says the abbreviation is removed from the word

parts.note: to suit is to befit

explanation.surface: A criminal wearing a suit, with the British angle ruled out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' drops B from BEFIT.
explanation.definitionFit: An electronic facial composite built from witness descriptions helps police identify a suspect.

parts.note: C is the cricket abbreviation for caught
a rook is a cheat or swindler

explanation.surface: A con artist on the payroll has been caught.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swindler' wants to be the definition; the answer means a swindler too, but here it is the shepherd's staff.
explanation.definitionFit: A shepherd's or bishop's hooked stick is a kind of staff.

clue.text: Activist — one spied round street by St Paul's

parts.note: Che Guevara, the revolutionary activist
A is a word for one

indicators.note: round suggests the letters are turned about into a new order

explanation.surface: A political activist spotted near a street by the cathedral.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' rearranges the one-letter word and 'spied' into APSIDE. Cheapside is a historic London street right beside St Paul's Cathedral.
explanation.definitionFit: The named London thoroughfare runs past the cathedral, so it is a street by that church.

clue.text: Inhuman robber baron demanded endless kinky sex

indicators.note: kinky means twisted, so these letters are bent into a new order
endless says the word loses its final letter

parts.note: IT is a crossword word for sex appeal

explanation.surface: A cruel baron demanding unusual sexual favours.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endless' trims DEMANDED to DEMANDE; 'kinky' rearranges BARON + DEMANDE into ONEARMEDBAND, and IT is added.
explanation.definitionFit: A fruit machine takes your money and is not a person, so it is a robber that is not human.

clue.text: Evil chief a topline criminal? He could be

definitions.text: Evil chief a topline criminal? He could be

indicators.note: criminal suggests the letters are crooked, set in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: An evil boss, a top criminal: maybe the main bad guy of the story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'criminal' rearranges all seventeen letters of EVIL CHIEF A TOPLINE; the whole clue also describes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The main wrongdoer in a story is an evil chief, an expression for the person most to blame.

indicators.note: reportedly says we want how the word for yes is said, not spelt

parts.note: aye is an old or dialect word for yes
RA, the Royal Artillery, are gunners who shoot

explanation.surface: The people who shoot are terrorists, apparently.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reportedly' gives I from the spoken AYE; RA is the Royal Artillery, British army gunners.
explanation.definitionFit: The Irish Republican Army was a paramilitary group widely labelled terrorists.

clue.text: English fit in somewhere in Surrey

parts.note: fit means healthy, well

explanation.surface: An English person settles in somewhere in Surrey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fit in' reads like settling in; 'fit' is just WELL and 'in' is a link. Ewell is a town in Surrey, a county south-west of London.
explanation.definitionFit: The named town lies in that county, so it is a place in Surrey.

clue.text: 'Jerk!' said Liberal briefly to fan of Nick

indicators.note: a jerk is a sudden jolt, so these letters are jolted into a new order

parts.note: Lib is the short form of Liberal

explanation.surface: Someone calls a Liberal named Nick's admirer a jerk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jerk!' looks like an insult but rearranges SAID + LIB + TO. Old Nick is a name for the Devil, so his fan is a devil-worshipper.
explanation.definitionFit: Old Nick is the Devil, and a devotee of the Devil is a devil-worshipper or Satanist.

clue.text: Studied for a degree after employment

indicators.note: after places the degree letter following the word for employment

parts.note: per means for each, for a
employment of something is its use

explanation.surface: Someone studied for a degree after starting a job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Studied for a degree' reads as one phrase, but the definition is 'Studied' alone.
explanation.definitionFit: To read something through carefully is to have studied it; a close synonym.

parts.note: the word maybe without its middle letter leaves MABE, which is the letters of BEAM jumbled; so the word beam, mixed up or 'off', gives these words

explanation.surface: Perhaps cruel and mistaken.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as an instruction: BEAM shuffled ('off') makes MABE, which is 'Maybe' without its heart, the Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Being wide of the mark or wrong is to be misguided; an informal synonym.

indicators.note: solved suggests the word is worked out and its letters undone into another order

parts.note: one gives AN and time gives T, the standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: Crimes cleared up by a former offender.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one-time' looks like 'former' but splits into AN (one) + T (time), after CRIMES rearranged by 'solved'.
explanation.definitionFit: A wrongdoer or villain is a criminal; a direct synonym.

indicators.note: accepted says the record is taken in by the abbreviation

parts.note: an EP, extended play, is a record

explanation.surface: An international record has been accepted as junk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'accepted' is the container signal; 'as' links. 'rubbish' here is the adjective, as in useless.
explanation.definitionFit: Clumsy and incompetent is what rubbish means in British slang, as in 'rubbish at football'.

parts.note: the other people, not us, are them

indicators.note: without says that letter is removed from the word

parts.note: to steal is to rob
R is the physics symbol for resistance

explanation.surface: Criminals, not people like us, steal without meeting resistance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' removes the resistance symbol from the verb, leaving OB; 'not us' is a playful way to say the others.
explanation.definitionFit: An organised gang of criminals is called by this term, especially the Mafia.

clue.text: Lots of laws passed — occasionally some rejected

indicators.note: rejected says the hidden letters are read backwards
some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Many laws are passed now and then; some get rejected.
explanation.definitionFit: Systematic collections of laws, like a penal or legal set, are such bodies of rules.

clue.text: Mineral on counter offender picked up

indicators.note: on places the sounded part beside the counter word
picked up means heard, so the word for offender is given by its sound

parts.note: a sinner is an offender
a bar is a counter in a pub

explanation.surface: A mineral sitting on a pub counter, and an offender being picked up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'picked up' gives CINNA, said like SINNER; then BAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Mercury sulphide is a red ore, a mineral used for the pigment vermilion.

parts.note: MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is a doctor's degree
a race is a competition

explanation.surface: A contest welcomed alongside a European physician.
explanation.walkthrough: MB is the British medical degree, used in crosswords for a doctor.
explanation.definitionFit: To accept or greet something gladly is to welcome it; a synonym verb.

clue.text: Drinking party not about to wake up

indicators.note: not says the letter for about is removed

parts.note: a carouse is a drinking party
C, circa, is an abbreviation for about

explanation.surface: A drinking party not about to wake up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' drops C from CAROUSE; 'to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To rouse or stir someone from sleep is to wake them up.

clue.text: Amusements here not just provided by female

parts.note: not just means not fair, unfair

explanation.surface: Amusements here are not merely laid on by a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not just' reads like 'not only' but means UNFAIR, after F.
explanation.definitionFit: A travelling fairground with rides and stalls is where amusements are found.

parts.note: a firm is slang for a criminal gang

indicators.note: emptied says the word loses its insides, leaving only its outer letters

explanation.surface: A gang of crooks cleared out a lorry quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fast' looks like quickly but means held tight.
explanation.definitionFit: Held fast means held securely, so fast here is an adverb for tightly or securely.

indicators.note: repairs suggests the letters are fixed up and put back in a new order

explanation.surface: A craftsman's job involves doing repairs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'repairs' rearranges ROLE DOING. 'Craftsman' is a pun: his craft is a Venetian boat.
explanation.definitionFit: A Venetian boatman works a craft, a boat, so he is a craftsman in a punning sense.

indicators.note: out says the letter for take is removed

parts.note: something that got bigger has grown
R, from Latin recipe, is the abbreviation for take

explanation.surface: Has the dress got too small? Let it out.
explanation.walkthrough: R is the prescription abbreviation for 'take'; 'out' removes it from GROWN.
explanation.definitionFit: A long formal frock is a kind of dress; a direct synonym noun.

indicators.note: attacked says the name is set upon and broken into a new order

explanation.surface: Tania assaulted another woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'attacked' rearranges TANIA; 'her' stands for a woman's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A girl's name stands for a female person, referred to by the pronoun in the clue.

clue.text: That man as indicated breaking law on return — odd

indicators.note: breaking says the other pieces split the reversed word open
on return says the word law is read backwards

parts.note: the word law itself
that man is him
sic, Latin 'thus', marks a quotation reproduced as indicated

explanation.surface: That man is breaking the law again as noted: strange.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on return' makes WAL, which 'breaking' splits open to hold the other two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Quirky and fanciful behaviour is odd; a playful synonym adjective.

clue.text: Talk of thieves taking money from girl

indicators.note: taking money from a person removes that letter
from names the girl's name as the word that loses the letter

parts.note: Margot is a girl's name

explanation.surface: Thieves' talk about taking cash off a girl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking ... from' removes M from MARGOT.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang or jargon used by a particular group, originally criminals, is that group's private language.
